UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                  )
    Southern Indiana Gas and Electric Company     )
    v. Midcontinent Independent System            )          Docket No. EL26-38-000
    Operator, Inc.                                )
                                                  )

    PROTEST OF THE SIERRA CLUB, ENVIRONMENTAL LAW & POLICY CENTER,
     CITIZENS ACTION COALITION OF INDIANA, CITIZENS UTILITY BOARD OF
     WISCONSIN, CITIZENS UTILITY BOARD OF ILLINOIS, AND PUBLIC CITIZEN

         Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 the Sierra

Club, Environmental Law & Policy Center, Citizens Action Coalition of Indiana, the Citizens

Utility Board of Wisconsin, Citizens Utility Board of Illinois, and Public Citizen (“Public

Interest Organizations” or “PIOs”) submit this response to the complaint of Southern Indiana

Gas and Electric Company (“SIGE”) against the Midcontinent Independent System Operator

(“MISO”) filed with the Commission on January 5, 2026 (“Complaint”).

         SIGE filed the Complaint in response to the December 23, 2025, Department of Energy

Order No. 202-25-13 (“Order”) requiring the continued operation of the coal-fired Unit 2 at the

F.B. Culley Generating Station (“Culley Unit 2” or “Unit 2”). The Order came just days before

SIGE planned to retire Unit 2. The Order declared that “an emergency exists in portions of the

Midwest region of the United States due to a shortage of electric energy, a shortage of facilities

for the generation of electricity, and other causes”2 and ordered SIGE and MISO to “take all

measures necessary to ensure that Culley Unit 2 is available to operate.”3 The Order further

   directed MISO to “take every step to employ economic dispatch of Culley Unit 2 to minimize

  cost to ratepayers.”4

           As detailed below, PIOs oppose SIGE’s complaint, which contradicts the Order, fails to

  identify any beneficiaries of Unit 2, and seeks compensation for an unlawful application of

  Federal Power Act (“FPA”) Section 202(c). The Commission should reject it.

I.         INTRODUCTION

           Culley Unit 2 is an outdated and unreliable coal-fired generator. Built in 1966, Unit 2 has

  been experiencing long and recurrent outages in recent years, with a forced outage rate of 32.4%

  in 2024.5 SIGE has repeatedly stated that Unit 2 is the “oldest, smallest, and least efficient”6 coal

  unit the utility owns and has planned for the retirement of Unit 2 for over a decade.7 Unit 2 has,

  in SIGE’s own words, “run past its useful life.”8 SIGE had therefore sought and received

  approval from MISO to retire Culley Unit 2 and was on track to close Unit 2 by December 31,

  2025.9

           The Order overturned that process in the final hours, making it the latest in a line of

  orders requiring continued operation of soon-to-retire gas- or coal-fired units across the country.

  Since last spring, the Department of Energy has relied on FPA Section 202(c) to prop up

  expensive plants across the country, overriding the resource planning decisions of states and

 nullifying the resource adequacy determinations of grid operators and state regulators.10 Far from

identifying the sort of discrete emergency that Congress envisioned with the enactment of FPA

Section 202(c),11 the Department has repeatedly relied on vague claims of generalized “energy

emergencies” to support its orders.12 The result is hundreds of millions of dollars in unnecessary

costs overall, and an estimated cost for Unit 2 net of market revenues of at least $2,121,000 over

the 90 day Order.13

         Like earlier orders, the Order misrepresents North American Electric Reliability

Corporation planning documents and MISO residual capacity auction results to conclude a) that

“an emergency exists in portions of the Midwest region of the United States due to a shortage of

electric energy”;14 and b) that these emergency conditions “will continue in the near term and are

also likely to continue in subsequent years.”15 These determinations fly in the face of all

available evidence—including evidence that the Order itself cites. Most telling is Department’s

citation of a June 2025 Organization of MISO States survey, which found that MISO will have a

“surplus of generation capacity” in 2026.16 That finding—which the Department quotes—

undercuts the Department’s emergency declaration.

          The Order directs SIGE’s and MISO’s operation of the plant: First, the Order says that

“MISO is directed to take every step to employ economic dispatch of Culley Unit 2 to minimize

cost to ratepayers.”17 Second, the Order says that “[b]ecause this Order is predicated on the

shortage of facilities for generation of electric energy and other causes, Culley Unit 2 shall not be

considered a capacity resource.”18

         SIGE’s complaint relies on FPA Section 202(c) to seek compensation for continued

operation of Unit 2. SIGE asks the Commission to allocate Unit 2’s costs across the MISO North

and Central regions based on the “load ratio share” of the load-serving entities in those regions.

SIGE states ”[c]urrently, there is no MISO Tariff provision that would permit SIGE’s costs of

complying with the DOE Order to be allocated to LSEs in MISO’s northern and central zones”

and that this “would effectively prevent SIGE from recovering its costs via FPA section

202(c).”19 SIGE does not seek a determination of “the specific costs, if any, to be recovered by

[SIGE],”20 instead stating that costs SIGE seeks to recover will be submitted to the Commission

in a separate proceeding at an as of yet undetermined time.21 SIGE does not provide any

indication of the dollar amount of costs it will eventually seek to recover, and instead states that

it intends to seek recovery for “Order Costs net of market revenues.”22

 II.               ARGUMENT

                  The Commission should reject SIGE’s complaint because ratepayers should not be

      subject to costs for unlawful 202(c) orders. The Commission should also reject SIGE’s complaint

      because SIGE fails to do the fundamental work needed to ensure a just and reasonable cost

      allocation methodology: showing that costs are allocated commensurate with benefits. SIGE

      does not identify any benefits Culley Unit 2 is providing to MISO North and Central customers

      that are not already compensated under existing provisions of the MISO tariff. Absent such a

      showing, there is no case for SIGE to recover any costs beyond those already provided for in

      current tariff provisions. And while SIGE identifies a class of beneficiaries, it does not attempt to

      show why its proposed cost allocation methodology—load ratio share—allocates costs

      commensurate with benefits within that class. This failure also warrants rejecting the SIGE

      complaint.

                  A.     The Commission Should Not Require Ratepayers to Fund Unlawful 202(c)
                         Orders.

                  SIGE asserts that it has a “statutory right to recover costs associated with the DOE

      Order” and that this right is evident in “the plain language of FPA section 202(c), the DOE

      Referral Regulation, and the DOE Order, itself.”23 SIGE does not allege any alternative need or

      legal basis for continuing to operate Culley Unit 2 and seeking “recovery of all costs for the

      continued operation of Culley Unit 2.”24 Thus, by the terms of SIGE’s complaint, the

      Commission’s authority to allocate costs to load-serving entities in MISO North and Central

      arises exclusively from the Order, which itself arises solely from Section 202(c).




      23
           Id. at 14.
      24
           Id. at 24.

                                                           5
         The Commission should not allow SIGE to recover costs associated with the Order

because it is unlawful. The Order addresses circumstances beyond the lawful scope of an

emergency under Section 202(c) and fails to provide evidence or reasoned decision-making

substantiating the existence of an emergency that can come within Section 202(c). The Order’s

primary focus is long-term bulk-system reliability, which is not a basis to mandate generation

under Section 202(c). Additionally, the Order does not, and could not, provide any valid

evidence or reasoned decision-making to support its stated near-term resource adequacy

concerns.

        Separately, the Order suffers from other legal deficiencies. These include (1) the failure

to exercise reasoned decision-making in imposing a requirement to “best meet” the claimed

emergency and serve the public interest; (2) the imposition of availability requirements beyond

the Department of Energy’s jurisdiction under Section 202(c); (3) the disallowance of capacity

market treatment without reasoned decision-making and beyond jurisdictional limits; and (4) the

failure to comply with limitations in Section 202(c)(2), including failing to “ensure” that the

Order requires generation only as needed to meet the claimed emergency and serve the public

interest.

        Given the facially evident legal shortcomings with the Order, the Commission should, at

a minimum, withhold any ruling on SIGE’s Complaint until legal challenges to the Order have

been exhausted. A subset of PIOs have challenged the Order and will, unless the Department

grants rehearing, subsequently have the opportunity to seek review at the D.C. Circuit Court of

Appeals. Should any party do so, the Commission should allow the courts to determine whether

the Order was lawful before approving a cost allocation methodology based on the Order. Even

if the Commission determines that creating a cost allocation mechanism is appropriate, however,


                                                 6
 the Commission should, at a minimum, make clear that any and all costs assigned pursuant to the

new tariff provision are subject to refund if the underlying 202(c) Order is found unlawful.

         B.       Any Cost Recovery that the Commission Approves Must Adhere to the Cost
                  Causation Principle.

         Most of the Commission’s electricity ratemaking takes place under the auspices of FPA

Sections 205 or 206, which charge the Commission with ensuring “just and reasonable” rates and

with rectifying “unjust and unreasonable” rates respectively.25 Courts have explained that this

just and reasonable standard is the basis for foundational ratemaking principles, including the

cost-causation principle, the rule against retroactive ratemaking, and the filed-rate doctrine.

         As the DC Circuit explains, the cost-causation principle requires that “in order to ensure

just and reasonable rates, FERC must make some reasonable effort to match costs to benefits.”26

In Illinois Commerce Commission v. FERC, the 7th Circuit held that, “FERC is not authorized to

approve a pricing scheme that requires a group of utilities to pay for facilities from which its

members derive no benefits, or benefits that are trivial in relation to the costs sought to be

shifted to its members.”27 The “cost-causation” and “beneficiary-pays” principles are two sides

of the same coin, with courts and the Commission applying them interchangeably.28 They both

public utility for or in connection with the transmission or sale of electric energy be just and reasonable. 16 U.S.C.S.
§ 824d(a). For decades, the FERC and the courts have understood this requirement to incorporate a cost-causation
principle.”); Long Island Power Auth. & Long Island Lighting Co. v. FERC, 27 F.4th 705, 709 (D.C. Cir. 2022)
(citing Midwest ISO Transmission Owners v. FERC, 373 F.3d 1361, 1368 (D.C. Cir. 2004)) (cleaned up) (“To be
just and reasonable, rates must ‘reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by the customer who must pay for
them.’ This ‘cost-causation principle’ requires ‘comparing the costs assessed against a party to the burdens imposed
or benefits drawn by that party.’”).

28

 make clear that, in order to set compensation that is just and reasonable, the Commission cannot

allocate a facility’s costs to ratepayers who receive no material benefit from the facility.

        While this ratemaking proceeding occurs under the auspices of a FPA Section 202(c)(1)

rather than the more common FPA Sections 205 or 206, the statute similarly provides that “the

Commission, after hearing held either before or after such order takes effect, may prescribe by

supplemental order such terms as it finds to be just and reasonable, including the compensation

or reimbursement which should be paid to or by any such party.”29 The just and reasonable

standard mandated by the FPA applies in the 202(c) cost allocation context as well, and carries

with it the bedrock “just and reasonable” derived ratemaking principles that the Commission

considers in Section 205 and 206 ratemaking cases.

        SIGE agrees that the cost-causation and beneficiary-pays principles should apply here.30

The Commission also recognized as much implicitly in the Campbell 202(c) cost allocation

proceeding. There, the Commission correctly emphasized that the cost-causation principle is a

relevant standard to apply in 202(c) recovery actions, 31 despite some parties arguing otherwise.32

Like in the Campbell 202(c) cost allocation order, the Commission must adhere to foundational

ratemaking principles derived from the just and reasonable standard in any order it issues in this

docket, including ensuring that any costs assigned are commensurate with the benefits.

        C.       Application of Traditional Ratemaking Principles, Including the Beneficiary
                 Pays Principle, Cannot Support SIGE’s Request for Broad Cost Recovery

        Applying these principles to the present circumstances reveals no basis for SIGE’s

request for broad cost recovery on the costs SIGE incurs in purported compliance with the Order.

 Generators in MISO are primarily compensated for capacity, energy, and operating reserves.33

As discussed further below, these payments are designed to provide compensation for generators

at a just and reasonable rate for their contributions to the grid. Culley Unit 2 cannot be

compensated for any capacity contributions unless the Commission disregards the Order,

because such a recovery would conflict with the Order’s directive that “Culley Unit 2 shall not

be considered a capacity resource.”34 There is reason to believe that SIGE can receive

compensation for the energy and ancillary services Culley Unit 2 provides.

       SIGE’s filing states that “the DOE Order… provide[s] for full cost recovery.”35 But the

Order does no such thing. The Order is clear that “[r]ate recovery is available pursuant to 16

U.S.C. § 824a(c).”36 Traditional ratemaking principles require that costs be allocated

commensurate with the benefits, and the Commission recognized the need to apply the principle

that costs be allocated commensurate with benefits in 202(c) contexts in cost allocation

proceedings for the Campbell plant.37 And as highlighted in the following section, MISO already

has tariff provisions that allocate the costs associated with Culley Unit 2’s energy and ancillary

services market participation. Absent a showing that the current tariff provisions will not

properly compensate SIGE for the benefits Culley Unit 2 provides to the grid, a new cost

allocation tariff provision is unjustified. And SIGE has not made that showing. PIOs expound on

each of these points in the following sections.

                  i.      Culley Unit 2 cannot be compensated for providing capacity.

        The Department Order is clear: “Because this Order is predicated on the shortage of

facilities for generation of electric energy and other causes, Culley Unit 2 shall not be considered

a capacity resource.”38 Unless the Commission disregards the Order, the Commission cannot

approve any compensation that arises from any capacity benefit from Unit 2. The Order did not

say, for example, that Culley Unit 2 “cannot participate in the capacity market,” in which case it

might still have provided capacity value outside of the market. Instead, the Department’s Order

categorically prohibits the unit from being considered a capacity resource. And without the

ability to recognize a corresponding benefit, it is not just and reasonable for the Commission to

assign costs associated with Culley Unit 2’s capacity value to any MISO participants.

        Beyond the dictates of the Order, there is an independent reason why FERC cannot

assign costs based on the capacity value of Culley Unit 2: load-serving entities in MISO have

already paid to acquire sufficient capacity for 2026, including a reserve margin, and will not

benefit materially from any additional capacity Culley Unit 2 provides. MISO’s 2025-2026

capacity auction procured sufficient generating supplies for both MISO as whole and Indiana

specifically.39 Culley Unit 2 did not participate in that auction, which means that its capacity is

not required for MISO to maintain adequate supplies plus a reserve margin. The Order itself

recognizes this reality, stating that MISO has a “small surplus of generation capacity in 2026”

without Culley Unit 2.40

        The unavailability of cost recovery for Culley Unit 2’s capacity offerings is particularly

relevant because SIGE itself has suggested that the basis for its proposed cost allocation is the

 capacity value of Culley Unit 2. Specifically, SIGE argues that order costs “should be allocated

regionally rather than only to the State of Indiana . . . . [because] SIGE customers are already

paying for the cost to fulfill the capacity needs of Zone 6.”41 This justification suggests that

SIGE’s conception of Culley Unit 2’s value centers on its capacity value: whether Zone 6 has

fulfilled its capacity needs is only relevant if the cost allocation methodology is based on Culley

Unit 2’s capacity offerings. Again, any assignment of costs based on the capacity value of Culley

Unit 2 is, as discussed above, prohibited by the terms of the Order.

                 ii.      MISO will already adequately compensate Culley Unit 2 for providing
                          energy and ancillary services.

        The Department 202(c) order directs MISO to employ economic dispatch of Culley Unit

2.42 And SIGE recognizes that it can collect market revenues in its filing.43 The cost allocation,

and level of compensation, for market participation are already well defined in the MISO tariff,44

and already operate to reimburse market participants fully for any services they provide. On top

of these standard energy market revenues, the MISO tariff is specifically designed to allow for

extremely high compensation to generators during periods of scarcity—levels of compensation

high enough that they meet or exceed the value of lost load. MISO has established (and the

Commission approved) energy and operating reserve payments that play a critical role in

ensuring resource adequacy in the region. In approving MISO’s resource adequacy construct, the

Commission recognized that in MISO, more so than in other RTOs, “the ancillary services

market, scarcity pricing and a long-term resource adequacy plan all play a role in ensuring

resource adequacy.”45 Specifically, the Commission noted that MISO’s scarcity pricing

        Nor could these existing cost-recovery mechanisms fairly be described as somehow

insufficient. This past April, the Commission approved tariff revisions that increased MISO’s

Value of Lost Load (“VOLL”) to $10,000/MWh.47 This price is a cap and serves as an

administratively set price during MISO-directed Energy Emergency Alert (EEA)-Level 3 load-

shed events.48 The Commission found that MISO’s $10,000/MWh price “reasonably estimates

the value residential loads place on avoiding load shedding.”49 As the Commission observed:

        “VOLL does guide investment and retirement decisions in the long term . . . [and]
        shortage price signals in the Day-Ahead and Real-Time markets, which are
        developed through the VOLL and [Operating Reserve Demand Curve], are also
        near-term signals to incent real-time actions by generation and demand resources
        during the Operating Day, or the day before the Operating Day, to avoid potential
        shortage conditions.”50

        In short, in the extremely unlikely event that MISO actually uses Culley Unit 2’s specific

energy production, or the even more unlikely event that this production helps MISO avoid or

lessen the impact of a reliability event that “[led] to the loss of power to homes and businesses in

the areas that may be affected by curtailments or power outages, presenting a risk to public

health and safety,”51 the MISO tariff already contains provisions that would fully compensate

SIGE for the value the Culley Unit 2 actually provides, at a rate that the Commission has

                 iii.     SIGE must specifically articulate any uncompensated services it
                          believes must be addressed per traditional ratemaking principles.

        To the extent SIGE feels additional recovery is necessary to ensure it is made whole for

costs incurred in compliance with the Order, SIGE must demonstrate that such recovery meets

the cost-causation principle. The Commission would then need to identity the benefits associated

with the costs and determine to whom the benefits flow. Only then can the Commission

determine who should be allocated costs. Providing such an analysis in the Commission’s order

is a necessary prerequisite to the reasoned decision-making required by the FPA and

Administrative Procedure Act.52

        The Commission has said that a similar Department 202(c) order issued for the Campbell

plant suggests that the scope of the emergency is in MISO zones 1-7. But even if the

Commission must accept the Order’s conclusion that 1) there is an emergency need, and 2) the

order addresses that need,53 the Commission still must articulate what the benefits associated

   In its order on cost allocation for costs associated with the Campbell 202(c), the Commission recognized that
“parties have presented different interpretations of how the Order defined the geographic scope of the emergency”
but determined that “the most reasonable reading of the Order’s intended scope is that the emergency necessitating
the continued operation of the Campbell Plant is in the MISO North and MISO Central regions, i.e., Local Resource
Zones 1-7. Specifically, we find that it is reasonable to interpret the Order’s reliance on statements in MISO’s
presentation on the Planning Resource Auction Results for Planning Year 2025-2026 that ‘new capacity additions
were insufficient to offset the negative impacts of decreased accreditation, suspension/retirements and external
resources’ in the MISO North and MISO Central regions as indicating that resource adequacy concerns for those
regions were the driver for the Order.” Consumers Energy Co. v. Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Op., Inc., 192 FERC ¶
61,158, at P 40 (2025). Even if the Commission cannot second guess the Department’s finding of an emergency and
need, the very recognition that the Department was not clear and there are multiple reasonable readings of the Order
recognizes that the Department did not speak preclusively on the matter of who the beneficiaries are. As such, the

                                                        13
        with the unit are in order to justify the relative level of benefits each of MISO zones 1-7 receive,

       and thus how to allocate costs among zones 1-7. The currently proposed load ratio share proposal

       suggests that the benefits are proportionally (or at least roughly proportionally) commensurate

       with load withdrawing from the MISO grid and in a manner that scales linearly with each

       average MW of electricity withdrawn. But SIGE does not justify that, and it is far from self-

       evident that benefits accrue in zone 1-7 in a way that is aligned roughly with load ratio share.

       SIGE must identify what the benefits are, not just who the beneficiaries are, in order for the

       Commission to make a reasoned determination that the costs are allocated among the

       beneficiaries in a manner that is roughly proportionate to the share of the benefits each

       beneficiary receives.

               Finally, in the event SIGE elects this path, the Commission should hold a hearing to

       discuss any evidence SIGE provides to substantiate beneficiaries. Whether the simultaneity of

       cost-based compensation and market-based compensation causes duplicative recovery, whether

       any duplicative recovery renders the filed rate unjust and unreasonable, and the extent to which

       different MISO participants benefit from Culley Unit 2 are genuine issues of material fact

       warranting a hearing,54 and in any event the Commission’s decision making would benefit from

       a broad variety of perspectives.

III.           CONCLUSION

               For the foregoing reasons, PIOs respectfully request that the Commission reject SIGE’s

       complaint.




       Commission has an obligation to independently make a determination as to who the beneficiaries are to ensure just
       cost allocation.
